The Torah Teaching, Scientific Work and Public Leadership of Rabbi Aviad Sar Shalom Basilea
This article surveys the life and teaching of Rabbi Aviad Sar Shalom Basilea, an exemplary figure of 18th-century Mantuan Jewry who embodied a unique synthesis of Torah scholarship and the exact sciences. The text presents Basilea as a Renaissance sage who combined halakha and Kabbalah with astronomy and mathematics, with an emphasis on his principal work, "Emunat Chakhamim" (Faith of the Sages), which was intended to defend the truth of the esoteric teaching against rationalism. Alongside his scientific and literary work, the source describes his courageous public leadership, expressed in his support for the Ramchal and in his firm stand against the persecutions of the Inquisition and the imprisonment imposed upon him. Ultimately, the work sketches a model of epistemological harmony, in which scientific knowledge serves as an instrument for understanding the Divine and for fortifying the walls of tradition.
The Torah Teaching, Scientific Work and Public Leadership of Rabbi Aviad Sar Shalom Basilea
Introduction: The Cultural and Intellectual Background of Mantuan Jewry
Italian Jewry at the beginning of the eighteenth century presented a unique model of cultural fusion, in which rigorous halakhic scholarship and deep engagement with the esoteric teaching existed alongside an exceptional openness to the exact sciences, philosophy and the natural sciences [cite: 1, 2, 3]. The Jewish community of Mantua was one of the liveliest centers of this cultural phenomenon [cite: 1, 2]. In this spiritual atmosphere grew the figure of Rabbi Aviad Sar Shalom Basilea, also known by his epithet "the Sar Shalom," who served as head of the rabbinic court (av beit din) and head of the yeshiva in Mantua [cite: 1, 2]. In his personality Basilea reflected the figure of the Jewish Renaissance sage: he was an accepted halakhic decisor, a Lurianic kabbalist of great stature, and at the same time an esteemed engineer, mathematician and astronomer who won a reputation among Christian circles and European men of science as well [cite: 1, 2, 3].
Biography and Spiritual Growth: His Family Roots and the Course of His Studies
Rabbi Aviad Sar Shalom Basilea was born in Mantua in 5440 (c. 1680) to an influential family of sages [cite: 1, 2]. His father, Rabbi Menachem Shimshon Basilea (d. 5453), was rabbi in Alessandria and afterwards served as chief rabbi of Mantua [cite: 2, 3]. The compound name given to him at birth, "Aviad Sar Shalom," was derived from the biblical verse in Isaiah 9, and expressed the intense messianic hopes that prevailed among his family and social circle in that turbulent period [cite: 2]. Already from the age of ten Rabbi Aviad began to study the various sciences in depth, and at the same time he immersed himself in the world of speculative Kabbalah through the teaching of Rabbi Moshe Cordovero (the Ramak) and the early theosophical books [cite: 2].
Rabbi Aviad acquired most of his Torah learning from the leading sages of the generation of Italian Jewry [cite: 1, 2]. He studied under the watchful eye of Rabbi Moshe Zacuto (the Ramaz), Rabbi Vitale Norzi, and members of the famous Segre family [cite: 2]. His principal teacher in Talmud and halakha was Rabbi Yehuda Briel [cite: 1, 2, 3]. In Kabbalah he attached himself to Rabbi Binyamin HaKohen Vitali (the Rabakh), who was one of the prominent disciples of the Ramaz [cite: 1, 3, 4]. His close companion on the school bench in his youth was Rabbi Yitzchak Lampronti, who was later to compose the first halakhic encyclopedia, "Pachad Yitzchak" [cite: 2, 3]. In 5489 (1729) Rabbi Aviad was formally ordained to the rabbinate and crowned as head of the rabbinic court and head of the yeshiva in Mantua, a position in which he in effect succeeded his father and led the community with a firm hand [cite: 1, 2, 3].

His Thought: "Emunat Chakhamim" and the Defense of the Kabbalistic Ship
The Theological Manifesto and the Book's Metaphors
Rabbi Aviad's exemplary work of thought, "Emunat Chakhamim," was first printed in Mantua in 5490 (1730), and received the approbations of the leading sages of the generation, among them Rabbi Yaakov Aboab and Nechemia ben Yaakov HaKohen [cite: 1, 2, 3]. The book was written out of a deep sense of mission to defend the tradition of Kabbalah against the waves of rationalism and skepticism [cite: 1, 3, 7]. On the book's title page were printed picturesque words defining the essence of the work as a holy meeting place, "heikha de-nashka ar'a de-oraita u-rekia de-chokhmeta ahadadei" – the place where the earth of the Torah and the heavens of scientific wisdom kiss one another [cite: 7].
Basilea uses dramatic and incisive metaphors to describe the opponents of Kabbalah [cite: 7]. He likens them to those swallowed up with Korah and his company, who with their mouths claim that "Moses and his Torah are true" but in their hearts are heretics and "they are liars" [cite: 7]. Kabbalistic wisdom itself he likens to a ship in the midst of a stormy sea, and its accusers he calls "tanina de-ka ba'ei le-mivla lah li-sfinta de-chokhmat ha-kabbalah" (the dragon/sea monster seeking to swallow the ship of Kabbalah) [cite: 7]. The book was intended to serve as a spiritual brake against those currents that sought to undermine the mystical character of the Torah [cite: 3].
The Question of the Authenticity of the Zohar and His Attitude to General Philosophy
One of the important methodological innovations in "Emunat Chakhamim" concerns the question of the authorship of the Book of the Zohar [cite: 3]. Rabbi Aviad presented a sophisticated intermediate position: he utterly rejected the claim that attributes the writing of the book to Rabbi Moshe de Leon as a forgery, yet at the same time he did not hold the naive view that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai physically wrote the book as we have it before us [cite: 3]. In his view, the theosophical core and the homilies in the book are indeed the authentic teaching of Rashbi, but it was transmitted orally from generation to generation among his disciples, and underwent editing and changes of wording until it was committed to writing at a later period [cite: 3].
To substantiate his arguments, Basilea incorporated into his work extensive knowledge of general philosophy and recorded quotations from the writings of Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle, Alexander of Aphrodisias, Averroes, Avicenna, Copernicus and Italian Renaissance thinkers such as Francesco Piccolomini and Ignazio Cotunio [cite: 2]. This combination was not intended to grant legitimacy to philosophical inquiry in itself, but to use the rational tools of philosophy in order to prove the truth of Kabbalah and its absolute superiority over limited human reason [cite: 1, 2, 3].
The Historiographical Controversy: Yaakov Emden's Glosses in the Book "Mitpachat Sefarim"
The sweeping defense of the Book of the Zohar and of Kabbalah that appears in "Emunat Chakhamim" aroused fierce opposition from sages who feared the strengthening of the Sabbatean movements, which were wont to rely on the language of the Zohar and its mystical expressions to justify grave halakhic transgressions [cite: 2, 8]. The sharpest critic of the book was Rabbi Yaakov Emden (the Yaavetz), who between 5488 and 5528 composed his monumental book "Mitpachat Sefarim" [cite: 3, 9, 10]. The book was first printed in 5528 (1768) at the Yaavetz's private printing press in Altona [cite: 3, 10].
The Yaavetz devoted a considerable part of his book to strictures and glosses on Basilea's "Emunat Chakhamim" [cite: 1, 2, 3]. In his burning zeal against the Sabbatean sect, the Yaavetz sought to prove that there are late passages and even forgeries that were planted in the Book of the Zohar, and that therefore it is not to be accepted in its entirety as holy and as ancient, from the Tannaitic period [cite: 8, 10]. This controversy caused a great storm in the Jewish world; the work "Mitpachat Sefarim" met with bans from various rabbis, while in a later period it was, of all people, adopted by the circles of the Maskilim (who printed it in a new edition in Lemberg in 5630, 1870), who saw in it a first-rate tool for the criticism of Scripture and of Kabbalah, even though the Yaavetz's original intention had been for the sake of Heaven and was meant to protect the walls of halakha [cite: 8, 10].
Science in the Service of the Sacred: His Astronomical and Engineering Activity
Rabbi Aviad Sar Shalom Basilea refused to see the general sciences as a threat to the world of Torah, and instead regarded them as necessary tools for understanding the wisdom of the Creator and for the practical application of halakha [cite: 1, 2, 3]. Already in his youth he acquired exceptional mastery of the exact sciences [cite: 1, 2, 3]. In 5456 (1696), when he was only about sixteen years old, he composed his astronomical work "Neyar ha-Yamim" (Neyer ha-Yamim), which remained in manuscript and was copied in several copies [cite: 2, 11]. The work included detailed astronomical tables ("Luchot ha-Po'el," the Tables of Po'el) based on the system of the Jewish-Catalan astronomer Jacob ben David ben Yom Tov (Po'el Bonet), alongside tables of half-daylight at latitude 44 north compiled by Mordechai Finzi [cite: 11].
In this manuscript Basilea demonstrated his scientific ability by making complex calendrical calculations applying the system of leap years ("bisestili") in order to align the Hebrew calendar with the Julian and Gregorian calendars [cite: 2, 11]. Among other things, he calculated the exact number of years that had elapsed from the creation of the world, through the historical Flood, up to the expulsion from Spain in 5252 (1492) [cite: 11]. His geometrical expertise also found expression in his editing and translation of Euclid's book "Elements" for his student and friend Avraham Segre [cite: 2, 3]. Despite his extensive engagement in these sciences, Basilea maintained a clear hierarchy in which philosophy and the general sciences are no more than "perfumers and cooks" to the infinite wisdom of the Torah [cite: 1].

Public Leadership, Halakhic Ruling and Confrontation with the Legal Authorities
Leading the Community and Proofreading Books
As the spiritual leader of Mantua, Rabbi Aviad worked tirelessly to restore religion to its proper state and to disseminate accurate Torah learning [cite: 1]. He developed a meticulous methodology of proofreading books and preparing them for print, out of the understanding that the errors of copyists and printers distort the understanding of halakha [cite: 1]. In the years 5483–5484 (1723–1724) he personally supervised the edition of the "Shulchan Arukh" volumes printed in Mantua, proofread them and added precise notes [cite: 1]. This work of his won wide recognition, and his halakhic responsa were incorporated into the collections of the leading sages of the generation, especially in the halakhic encyclopedia "Pachad Yitzchak" by his friend Rabbi Yitzchak Lampronti, which brings much testimony to his practical rulings [cite: 1, 2, 3].
The Ramchal Affair and the Confrontation with the Inquisition
Rabbi Aviad's public leadership was tested in the difficult moments of the Ramchal controversy (Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto) [cite: 1, 2, 3]. While most of the rabbis of Germany and Poland and some of the rabbis of Venice launched a sharp attack on the Ramchal and accused him of disguised Sabbateanism because of the revelations of his maggid, Rabbi Aviad was among the handful of leaders who defended him openly and courageously [cite: 1, 2, 3]. Basilea recognized in the Ramchal a true kabbalist acting out of holiness and purity, and this position of his stemmed directly from his teaching in the book "Emunat Chakhamim," which demands full trust in the hidden sages of the generation [cite: 3, 7].
This courageous stand alongside mystical figures, combined with his keeping an extensive library of books that had not passed under the supervising eye of the Christian censor, made Rabbi Aviad a target for the authorities of the Catholic Inquisition in Mantua [cite: 2, 3, 11]. In June 1733 a warrant was issued for his arrest on charges of possessing forbidden Hebrew books and uttering words of mockery against the Christian faith [cite: 2, 3, 11]. He was arrested and held in prison for almost a year [cite: 2, 3]. Because of a severe deterioration in his health, he was transferred in May 1734 to house arrest in his home in the ghetto [cite: 2, 3]. Only in June 1738 was his final sentence pronounced: three years of house arrest, a penalty that was commuted in 1739 by the Curia of Rome to a permanent restriction of movement within the bounds of the Mantua ghetto alone [cite: 2, 3]. Despite the deprivation of his physical freedom and his harsh restrictions, Rabbi Aviad continued to teach Torah, to answer halakhic questions and to engage in proofreading books until his last day [cite: 1, 2].
Summary and Conclusions
Rabbi Aviad Sar Shalom Basilea is an exemplary historical figure who embodies the golden age of Jewish-Italian wisdom [cite: 1, 4]. In days when the first cracks began to appear between the world of traditional faith and the world of modern science, Rabbi Aviad offered an alternative of integration and epistemological harmony [cite: 1, 2, 3]. His teaching in his book "Emunat Chakhamim" laid a stable theological foundation for the defense of the esoteric teaching, while conducting a respectful dialogue with general philosophy and with the achievements of modern science such as the Copernican system [cite: 2, 3].
His scientific and Torah work, from the writing of the astronomical tables in "Neyar ha-Yamim" at the age of sixteen to the proofreading of the Shulchan Arukh and his approbation of the Masoretic book "Minchat Shai," attests to a holistic conception that sees scientific and textual precision as an inseparable part of the service of God [cite: 1, 2, 11]. His firm stand alongside the Ramchal and the heavy personal price he paid by sitting in the prison of the Inquisition highlight his public courage and his absolute loyalty to emunat chakhamim, faith in the sages, in practice [cite: 2, 3]. His multifaceted legacy remains one of the most splendid links between the world of halakha, mysticism and modern science [cite: 1, 2, 3].
